In Praise of the Unfinished List

Jonah Okafor — Essays

For about ten years I kept a document called "To read". It started as a handful of links I meant to get back to on a quiet Sunday, and it ended as a scroll of four thousand items that I could not open without a small wave of guilt. Every entry had seemed urgent once. Most of them I could no longer place. Some of the sites had disappeared entirely, and with them whatever argument or story had made me pause.

The list did not fail because I am lazy, or because I lacked a better app. It failed because it had no edges. Nothing ever left it except by my effort, and my effort was always going somewhere else. A list that can only grow is not a plan. It is a record of what I once wanted to be the kind of person who reads.

The cost of keeping everything

We tend to think of saving as free. A tap, a bookmark, a share to some inbox, and the thing is safe. But every saved item makes a small claim on the future. It says: one day you will spend twenty minutes on me. Multiply that by a few thousand and you have committed years of evenings you do not have. The debt is invisible until you open the list, and then it is all you can see.

There is a second cost, subtler than the first. When everything is kept, nothing is chosen. The act of saving replaces the act of reading, and the pleasure of the first starts to stand in for the second. I noticed that I would save an essay, feel a little lift of virtue, and move on. The essay had done its job for me without my reading a word of it.

Libraries know this. A library that never weeded its shelves would be unusable within a generation. Librarians pull books that have not circulated, that are out of date, that are duplicated elsewhere, and they do it without sentiment because the collection serves readers, not the other way round. My list had no librarian. It had only a hoarder with good intentions.

What a limit gives back

Last year I tried something different. I allowed myself ten things at a time, and each one had a week. If I had not read it in seven days, it went. Not to an archive, not to a folder called "later": it went, and I let it. The first week was uncomfortable. I kept wanting to save just one more, and the rule made me decide which of the ten I cared about least.

That decision turned out to be the whole point. Choosing what to drop forced me to ask why I had saved anything at all. Some links were there because a person I admire had shared them. Some were there because the headline flattered an opinion I already held. A few were there because I genuinely wanted to understand something, and those were the ones I found I actually read.

By the third week the anxiety had gone. Ten items is a number you can hold in your head. You know roughly what is waiting, and roughly how long it will take. When something expires, it is usually something you would not have read anyway, and seeing it go is a relief rather than a loss. The list stopped being a debt and became a small, pleasant queue.

Reading to the end

The other change was harder to predict. With fewer things waiting, I started finishing what I began. Before, an essay was always competing with the four thousand others behind it; any dull paragraph was an excuse to skip ahead to something that might be better. Now there were only nine others, all of which I had chosen deliberately, and the urge to abandon a piece halfway faded.

Finishing matters more than I expected. The last third of a good essay is often where the argument turns, where the writer stops setting up and starts saying the thing they came to say. Skim the opening and skip the end, and you have read the throat-clearing and missed the point. I had been doing this for years and calling it keeping up.

I also started writing down one sentence after each piece: the single idea I wanted to keep. It is a small habit, but it changes how you read. Knowing you will have to name the takeaway makes you look for it, and looking for it makes you notice when there isn't one. Some essays I had saved with real excitement turned out to have nothing in them I wanted to keep. That was useful to learn too.

Letting go well

None of this is a system, exactly. It is closer to a temperament, one that accepts that most of what we might read we never will, and that this is fine. The world produces more good writing every day than any one person could read in a year. Trying to keep up with it is like trying to drink a river. The sensible thing is to take a cup, drink it slowly, and let the rest flow past.

I still save things. I still feel the old pull of the infinite list when a particularly good week of writing comes along. But I have learned to trust the limit more than the impulse. The limit has never once made me miss something I later wished I had read. The impulse, left alone, buried hundreds of things I would have loved under thousands I did not need.

If you have a list like my old one, you do not need to read it. You do not even need to sort it. You can let it go, start again with ten, and give each of them a week. What you lose, you will not miss. What you keep, you might finally read to the end.
